title: Lecture 2 — Instructor Tutorial
subject: Algorithm Analysis
description: 11 questions transcribed from the instructor’s Tutorial 2: Asymptotic proofs, growth rates, and insertion-sort case behaviours. Source questions, choices, and answer-key selections are preserved.

questions.question: Based on the formal definition of Big-Ω, which of the following must be true for f(n) ∈ Ω(g(n))?
options: ∃c > 0, n₀ > 0 such that f(n) ≤ c ⋅ g(n) for all n ≥ n₀
∃c > 0, n₀ > 0 such that f(n) ≥ c ⋅ g(n) for all n ≥ n₀
f(n) represents the exact average-case growth.
f(n) is always strictly greater than g(n) for all values of n
questions.correctAnswer: ∃c > 0, n₀ > 0 such that f(n) ≥ c ⋅ g(n) for all n ≥ n₀
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects B: ∃c > 0, n₀ > 0 such that f(n) ≥ c ⋅ g(n) for all n ≥ n₀

questions.question: Big-Θ (Tight Bound) only exists for a function if:
options: The algorithm has no best-case or worst-case scenarios.
The input size n is a constant value.
Both the upper bound (Big-O) and lower bound (Big-Ω) match on the same dominant growth function.
The constant c is equal to 1.
questions.correctAnswer: Both the upper bound (Big-O) and lower bound (Big-Ω) match on the same dominant growth function.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects C: Both the upper bound (Big-O) and lower bound (Big-Ω) match on the same dominant growth function.

questions.question: If an algorithm has a tight bound of Θ(n²), which of the following is a valid statement regarding its Big-O and Big-Ω sets?
options: O(f(n)) can be n, and Ω(f(n)) can be n³
O(f(n)) can be n² or n³, and Ω(f(n)) can be n² or n
Both O(f(n)) and Ω(f(n)) must be exactly n² only
O(f(n)) must be 1, and Ω(f(n)) must be n!
questions.correctAnswer: O(f(n)) can be n² or n³, and Ω(f(n)) can be n² or n
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects B: O(f(n)) can be n² or n³, and Ω(f(n)) can be n² or n

questions.question: Arrange the following functions in increasing order of growth rate as per the lecture hierarchy: n!, 2ⁿ, n log n, nᵏ, 1, log n
options: 1 < log n < n log n < nᵏ < 2ⁿ < n!
1 < log n < nᵏ < n log n < 2ⁿ < n!
n! < 2ⁿ < nᵏ < n log n < log n < 1
1 < n log n < log n < 2ⁿ < nᵏ < n!
questions.correctAnswer: 1 < log n < n log n < nᵏ < 2ⁿ < n!
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects A: 1 < log n < n log n < nᵏ < 2ⁿ < n!

questions.question: To prove that f(n) = 3n² + 17n log n + 1000 ∈ O(n²), the lecture demonstrates combining terms to find constants. What are the resulting c and n₀ values used in the final step of this proof?
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects C: c = 1020, n₀ = 2

questions.question: When proving Big-Ω for a polynomial function, what is the recommended strategy?
options: Overestimate smaller terms with larger ones.
Ignore positive smaller terms and keep only the dominant (fastest-growing) term.
Multiply all coefficients together to find the constant c.
Choose n₀ to be the smallest possible integer.
questions.correctAnswer: Ignore positive smaller terms and keep only the dominant (fastest-growing) term.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects B: Ignore positive smaller terms and keep only the dominant (fastest-growing) term.

questions.question: If the input array provided to the Insertion Sort algorithm is already sorted, what is its runtime behavior?
options: It remains Θ(n²) because of the nested loops.
It achieves its Best-case behavior (Linear).
It achieves its Worst-case behavior (Quadratic).
The algorithm will fail to execute.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects B: It achieves its Best-case behavior (Linear).

questions.question: What happens to the time complexity of Insertion Sort when the input array is reverse-sorted?
options: It becomes O(log n)
It becomes O(n)
It becomes O(n²)
The complexity remains constant O(1)
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects C: It becomes O(n²)

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding f(n) = 2ⁿ and g(n) = 10n² is TRUE?
options: f(n) = O(g(n)), because 10n² has a larger coefficient.
f(n) = Ω(g(n)), because exponential growth eventually exceeds quadratic growth.
f(n) = Θ(g(n)), because both grow as n increases.
f(n) is slower growing than g(n).
questions.correctAnswer: f(n) = Ω(g(n)), because exponential growth eventually exceeds quadratic growth.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects B: f(n) = Ω(g(n)), because exponential growth eventually exceeds quadratic growth.

questions.question: Determine the correctness of this statement: f(n) = n is O(g(n)) where g(n) = 10.
options: True, because 10 is a constant.
True, because n can be smaller than 10.
False, because a linear function grows faster than a constant function.
False, because the coefficient 10 must be ignored.
questions.correctAnswer: False, because a linear function grows faster than a constant function.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects C: False, because a linear function grows faster than a constant function.

questions.question: Find the Big-O for the function f(n) = 50n log n + 20n
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects B: O(n log n)
